title: Animation & graphics in Compose
scopeHtml: Scope: animate*AsState, Transition, AnimatedVisibility/Content, Animatable, specs, phase-aware reads, graphicsLayer, Canvas/DrawScope, shared elements, animation jank. Version notes are from developer.android.com animation docs as read; items marked "verify" were not confirmed in a source.

questions.promptHtml: What does animateFloatAsState actually do? What is it built on, and what happens if the target changes mid-animation?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you know the high-level APIs are wrappers over Animatable and that animation is driven by recomposition by default.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I give it a target value and it returns a State that moves toward that target. Underneath it remembers an Animatable at the call site, runs it in a coroutine tied to the composition, and each frame writes the new value to snapshot state. If the target changes mid-flight it does not restart from the old start value. It retargets from the current value and current velocity, so the motion stays continuous.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
First principles: an animation is a value that changes over time. In Compose the "value over time" must live in snapshot state so reads are tracked. animate*AsState is remember { Animatable(initial) } plus a LaunchedEffect(target) that calls animateTo(target, spec). The first target is the initial value, so there is no animation on first composition.

target change -> LaunchedEffect restarts -> animateTo(new target)
                 (old run cancelled; Animatable keeps value + velocity)
each frame: withFrameNanos -> value written to State -> readers invalidated

The returned State.value is read where you use it. If you read it in the composable body, that scope recomposes every frame for the duration. If you read it inside a draw/layout lambda, only that phase reruns (see the phase-aware reads question). Built-in overloads: Float, Color, Dp, Size, Offset, Rect, Int, IntOffset, IntSize; anything else via animateValueAsState and a TwoWayConverter. The label parameter exists for Animation Preview and tooling only.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Fade(enabled: Boolean) {
    // Broken for perf at scale: read in composition body -> recomposes per frame
    val alpha by animateFloatAsState(if (enabled) 1f else 0.5f, label = "alpha")

    Box(
        Modifier
            .fillMaxSize()
            // Better: read in the draw/layer phase via the lambda form
            .graphicsLayer { this.alpha = alpha }
            .background(Color.Red)
    )
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Expecting an animation on first composition. The initial value equals the first target, so nothing animates.
  • Using it for state that must be driven by touch. It is target-based; for per-frame finger control use Animatable.snapTo.
  • Reading the delegated value in the composable body for a large subtree.
  • Forgetting that animate*AsState cannot be awaited; you cannot sequence animations with it.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you start an animation on first composition? → Start from a different initial value with Animatable + LaunchedEffect(Unit), or MutableTransitionState with rememberTransition.
  2. How do you know when it finished? → finishedListener parameter; or use Animatable/Transition where completion is a suspension point or currentState == targetState.
  3. What does it do to a running animation when the composable leaves composition? → The LaunchedEffect coroutine is cancelled and the animation stops.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer: "animates a value to a target." The senior adds: it is Animatable under a LaunchedEffect, it retargets with velocity continuity, and the cost model is that the State read location decides which phases rerun every frame.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A card list used animateColorAsState read in Modifier.background(color) on 30 visible items; every selection change recomposed all of them per frame until the read moved to drawBehind.

questions.promptHtml: When would you pick spring over tween? What are their defaults, and why does it matter when the user interrupts an animation?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests understanding of physics-based vs duration-based animation and why Compose defaults to springs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: tween is duration plus easing curve; it has a fixed end time. spring is physics: damping ratio and stiffness, no fixed duration, and it keeps velocity when the target changes. Compose uses spring as the default spec for animate*AsState and updateTransition because interruptions stay smooth. I use tween for choreographed, timed motion (fade in 150 ms, brand motion) and spring for anything the user can interrupt or drag.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A tween(durationMillis, delayMillis, easing) maps time fraction 0..1 through an Easing function. If the target changes at 40 percent, a tween restarts a new curve from the current value, but it starts with zero velocity, so you see a hitch: velocity discontinuity. A spring(dampingRatio, stiffness) solves a damped oscillator; when the target changes the new spring starts with the current position and velocity, so the curve is C1 continuous.

Spec Defined by Duration Interrupt behaviour
tween duration, easing, delay fixed restarts, velocity lost
spring dampingRatio, stiffness emergent velocity preserved
keyframes values at timestamps fixed like tween
snap none 0 jumps
repeatable / infiniteRepeatable wraps a duration-based spec n x n/a

Defaults per the docs: dampingRatio default is Spring.DampingRatioNoBouncy, stiffness default Spring.StiffnessMedium. Numeric values (1f and 1500f respectively) are from the API reference as I remember them: verify. Also verify tween default (300 ms, FastOutSlowInEasing). spring stops when within visibilityThreshold of the target, which matters for Dp/Offset types (otherwise it could spend many frames sub-pixel).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val x by animateDpAsState(
    targetValue = if (open) 240.dp else 0.dp,
    animationSpec = spring(
        dampingRatio = Spring.DampingRatioMediumBouncy,
        stiffness = Spring.StiffnessLow
    ),
    label = "drawerX"
)
val fade by animateFloatAsState(
    targetValue = if (visible) 1f else 0f,
    animationSpec = tween(durationMillis = 150, easing = LinearOutSlowInEasing),
    label = "fade"
)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using tween for a user-interruptible sheet and then blaming "janky" interruption.
  • Springs with bounce on a value that must not overshoot (alpha beyond 1, Dp below 0): alpha overshoot gets clamped by layer, but a negative size crashes or misbehaves. Use DampingRatioNoBouncy there.
  • Assuming a spring has a duration you can set. Use tween when design specs fix a duration.
  • infiniteRepeatable with a spring: only duration-based specs are allowed inside.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is there no duration on a spring? → Duration emerges from damping and stiffness; it ends when position and velocity are within thresholds.
  2. How do you make a bounce but end exactly on target? → Spring settles at the target; overshoot is transient. Clamp with coerceIn at the use site if the type cannot overshoot.
  3. How do tests treat infiniteRepeatable? → Per the docs, with ComposeTestRule such animations do not run and the initial value is rendered.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "spring is bouncy, tween is timed." Senior: velocity continuity on interruption, spec defaults, visibilityThreshold, and picking by whether designers fixed a duration.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A bottom sheet using tween(300) snapped back stiffly when users flicked it mid-open; switching to a spring removed the complaint without changing any design token.

questions.promptHtml: You have a card with expand/collapse that changes color, elevation, and arrow rotation together. Would you use three animate*AsState calls or updateTransition? Why?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Looks for knowing when state-driven coordinated animation is better expressed as a single Transition.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: updateTransition. One state drives all child animations, so they share a clock, can be inspected in Animation Preview, can have per-transition specs, and can be observed for completion. animate*AsState is fine for one independent value; with three values from one state I want a single source of truth and a single completion signal.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
updateTransition(targetState) returns a Transition<S> remembered at the call site. Each transition.animateX(label) { state -> value } creates a child animation. All children advance with the same transition state. You can set transitionSpec = { ... } per child, using A isTransitioningTo B for direction-specific specs. transition.currentState == transition.targetState means finished (docs). Transition.AnimatedVisibility and Transition.AnimatedContent let nested enter/exit animations join the same transition; createChildTransition splits it for sub-components. rememberTransition(MutableTransitionState) lets you start in a different initial state, for example animate on first composition.

state: Collapsed|Expanded ──> Transition ──> color  (spring)
                                          ├─> elevation (tween 200)
                                          └─> rotation  (tween 200)
                         one completion signal; one preview timeline

Trade-off: Transition is state-enumerated, so interrupt-safe retargeting still works (children retarget), but it is overkill for a single value or for gesture-driven values (use Animatable).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
enum class CardState { Collapsed, Expanded }

@Composable
fun ExpandCard(state: CardState) {
    val t = updateTransition(state, label = "card")
    val color by t.animateColor(label = "color") {
        if (it == CardState.Expanded) Color(0xFF6650A4) else Color(0xFFEADDFF)
    }
    val elevation by t.animateDp(label = "elev") {
        if (it == CardState.Expanded) 8.dp else 1.dp
    }
    val rotation by t.animateFloat(
        transitionSpec = { tween(200) },
        label = "arrow"
    ) { if (it == CardState.Expanded) 180f else 0f }

    Surface(color = color, shadowElevation = elevation) {
        Icon(
            Icons.Default.KeyboardArrowDown, null,
            Modifier.graphicsLayer { rotationZ = rotation }
        )
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Three separate animate*AsState driven by the same boolean, then wondering why completion callbacks fire at different times.
  • Forgetting label; Animation Preview then shows anonymous tracks.
  • Creating a new Transition each recomposition by not using updateTransition/rememberTransition.
  • Using animateFloatAsState for the exit part of AnimatedVisibility; the docs say AnimatedVisibility cannot account for it and may remove content early. Use transition.animate* inside the scope.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you animate on first composition with Transition? → rememberTransition(MutableTransitionState(initial).apply { targetState = x }).
  2. How do you share one transition between sub-composables? → createChildTransition { it == X } to give each a Transition<Boolean>.
  3. How do you encapsulate? → A holder class of State values returned from an updateXData composable, remembered on the transition (pattern in the docs).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average lists the API. Senior argues single source of truth, shared timeline/completion, per-direction specs, and the pitfall with exit animations that live outside the Transition.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checkout row with separate animations occasionally ended with color done but rotation mid-way after rapid taps; moving to one transition removed the half-states.

questions.promptHtml: Compare AnimatedVisibility, AnimatedContent, Crossfade and animateContentSize. When do you use which, and what is the one rule you must follow in AnimatedContent's lambda?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates use if (visible) with no animation or misuse AnimatedContent; this checks API selection and a classic bug.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: AnimatedVisibility is for one child appearing/disappearing, AnimatedContent for swapping content by a target state (with size animation), Crossfade for a plain fade between two states, and animateContentSize for a container whose size changes because its content changed. In AnimatedContent, always use the lambda parameter, not the outer variable, because the API uses the target value as the key identifying the content it is currently showing.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
AnimatedVisibility drives EnterTransition/ExitTransition (combined with +). By default it fades and expands in, fades and shrinks out. It keeps the child composed until the exit finishes, then removes it. Its content lambda has transition so custom animations join the exit; independent animate*AsState ones do not, and the content may be removed early (per docs).

AnimatedContent(targetState) keeps both initial and target content composed during the transition. Default is fade through. transitionSpec returns ContentTransform via enter togetherWith exit, optionally using SizeTransform. By default the target is drawn on top of the initial; change with targetContentZIndex; ExitTransition.KeepUntilTransitionsFinished keeps the old content until both transitions finish.

animateContentSize is a layout modifier. Docs: put it before size modifiers (size, defaultMinSize) so it reports the animated size.

API Use when Both contents composed?
AnimatedVisibility show/hide one thing child only, until exit ends
AnimatedContent swap by state, size change yes, during transition
Crossfade simple fade between states yes
animateContentSize own size changes n/a

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
var count by remember { mutableIntStateOf(0) }
AnimatedContent(
    targetState = count,
    transitionSpec = {
        if (targetState > initialState) {
            (slideInVertically { it } + fadeIn()) togetherWith
                (slideOutVertically { -it } + fadeOut())
        } else {
            (slideInVertically { -it } + fadeIn()) togetherWith
                (slideOutVertically { it } + fadeOut())
        }.using(SizeTransform(clip = false))
    },
    label = "counter"
) { target ->
    Text("$target") // not `count`
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reading outer count inside the lambda: the outgoing content then shows the new value during exit, so the animation looks like nothing changed.
  • Putting animateContentSize() after .height(...): size jumps because the modifier never observes the animated constraint.
  • Using AnimatedContent for a nullable loading/content/error flow and keeping heavy state inside; both children are composed at once during the transition.
  • Wrapping LazyColumn items in AnimatedVisibility for reorder; use Modifier.animateItem() (see lazy list chunk).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to give children their own enter/exit? → Modifier.animateEnterExit inside the scope; set parent to EnterTransition.None/ExitTransition.None if you want children only.
  2. How to observe visibility state? → AnimatedVisibility(visibleState = MutableTransitionState) exposes isIdle, currentState.
  3. Why is the old content drawn under or over? → Z-order default and targetContentZIndex.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average names the APIs. Senior states the lambda-key rule, double-composition cost, transition for custom exit animations and modifier ordering.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An OTP timer showed the new digit immediately and the animated ghost was invisible: the lambda used the captured state instead of the parameter.

questions.promptHtml: When do you reach for Animatable instead of animate*AsState? What are snapTo, animateTo, animateDecay and stop, and how do they behave when called concurrently?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Gesture-driven animation (swipe to dismiss, drag with fling) is where senior candidates separate themselves.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Whenever the animation is not just "state to target": I need an initial value different from the target, to sequence animations, to drive the value by touch, or to fling. Animatable is a value holder with suspend functions. It enforces mutual exclusion: starting a new animateTo cancels the one running and continues from the current value and velocity. snapTo sets the value instantly, which is what I use in drag handlers; animateDecay flings from a velocity.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Animatable<T, V> holds value (snapshot-backed), targetValue, velocity, isRunning. animateTo and animateDecay are suspend; they are called from a coroutine (LaunchedEffect, rememberCoroutineScope in event handlers, or inside pointerInput's scope). Both use a MutatorMutex-style policy: a new mutating call cancels the previous one, so value is always continuous. snapTo also cancels a running animation, which is why you can drag a card mid-animation and the finger takes over.

finger down:   scope.launch { anim.stop() } / snapTo(...) on each drag delta
finger up:     velocity from VelocityTracker
               decay = exponentialDecay().calculateTargetValue(anim.value, v)
               if decay passes threshold -> animateDecay / animateTo(edge)
               else animateTo(0f, spring)

Bounds: updateBounds(lower, upper) clamps value and lets decay stop at a bound.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun SwipeCard(onDismiss: () -> Unit) {
    val offsetX = remember { Animatable(0f) }
    Box(
        Modifier
            .offset { IntOffset(offsetX.value.roundToInt(), 0) } // layout phase read
            .pointerInput(Unit) {
                val decay = splineBasedDecay<Float>(this)
                coroutineScope {
                    while (true) {
                        val down = awaitPointerEventScope { awaitFirstDown().id }
                        offsetX.stop()
                        val tracker = VelocityTracker()
                        awaitPointerEventScope {
                            horizontalDrag(down) { change ->
                                val dx = change.positionChange().x
                                launch { offsetX.snapTo(offsetX.value + dx) }
                                tracker.addPosition(change.uptimeMillis, change.position)
                                change.consume()
                            }
                        }
                        val v = tracker.calculateVelocity().x
                        val target = decay.calculateTargetValue(offsetX.value, v)
                        launch {
                            if (abs(target) > size.width) {
                                offsetX.animateDecay(v, decay); onDismiss()
                            } else offsetX.animateTo(0f, initialVelocity = v)
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
    )
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Launching animateTo per drag event instead of snapTo; each launch cancels the previous and fights the finger.
  • Creating Animatable without remember, resetting every recomposition.
  • Doing fling math without velocity from VelocityTracker.
  • Running animateTo from LaunchedEffect with a changing key while also calling snapTo from a gesture: two writers.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What happens to a CancellationException in animateTo? → It propagates like any coroutine cancellation; do not swallow it, and note code after animateTo does not run when cancelled.
  2. How do you animate a custom type? → Provide a TwoWayConverter to Animatable.
  3. How do you run two Animatables in sync? → Launch both in the same scope; or use Transition.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "Animatable is lower-level." Senior: single-writer discipline, snapTo during drag, velocity-preserving retarget, decay with bounds, and phase-correct reads of .value.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A swipe-to-archive row stuttered because each onDrag launched animateTo(…, tween(0)); replacing it with snapTo fixed finger lag.

questions.promptHtml: An animated value changes every frame. How do you stop the whole composable (and its children) from recomposing on every frame? Explain which phase each approach reads in.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: This is the single most valuable animation performance idea in Compose; interviewers check you understand the three phases, not just "use remember".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Compose has composition, layout and draw. Whichever phase reads the State is the phase that reruns when it changes. If I read an animated value in the composable body, I recompose per frame. If I read it inside a lambda that executes in layout (Modifier.offset { }, layout {}) or draw (drawBehind { }, graphicsLayer { }), only that phase reruns and composition is skipped. So I pass lambdas or the State object down and read it as late as possible.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Snapshot reads are tracked by the observer active at read time: composition reads invalidate recompose scopes; reads in layout blocks invalidate the layout node (remeasure/relayout); reads in draw blocks invalidate only the draw (or the layer if inside graphicsLayer). The docs state: "be suspicious if you are causing recomposition just to re-layout or redraw" and "when passing frequently changing State variables into modifiers, use the lambda versions."

Read location Reruns Example
composable body composition, layout, draw Modifier.offset(x = dp) with x read in body
layout lambda layout, draw Modifier.offset { IntOffset(..) }
draw lambda draw only drawBehind { drawRect(color) }
graphicsLayer lambda layer property update (render thread), no relayout graphicsLayer { alpha = a }

Techniques: (1) hoist read into lambda parameter () -> Float; (2) pass the State<Float> itself, not .value; (3) use lambda modifiers. A Kotlin lambda passed to a child is stable/memoized (strong skipping on) so passing { scroll.value } does not re-trigger the child.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Recomposes Title every frame
@Composable fun Title(scroll: Int) =
    Column(Modifier.offset(y = scroll.dp)) { /*...*/ }

// Layout phase only
@Composable fun Title(scrollProvider: () -> Int) =
    Column(Modifier.offset { IntOffset(0, scrollProvider()) }) { /*...*/ }

// Draw phase only
val color by animateColorAsState(target, label = "c")
Box(Modifier.drawBehind { drawRect(color) }) // `color` read inside the lambda

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• val c by animate... then Modifier.background(c): the delegate read happens in the body, so the scope recomposes per frame. The lambda captures the delegate, and reads inside the lambda are the deferred ones.
  • Wrapping in remember { derivedStateOf } unnecessarily; it does not move the read to another phase.
  • Believing Modifier.alpha(x) is cheap; it recomposes to update. graphicsLayer { alpha = x } is the deferred version.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a lambda modifier skip layout too? → Draw-only reads skip layout; offset {} reads in layout, so layout reruns but not composition.
  2. How do you verify? → Layout Inspector recomposition counts, composition tracing.
  3. Why is it still sometimes recomposing? → The State is also read elsewhere in the body (e.g. in an if).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use remember and derivedStateOf." Senior maps each modifier to a phase and verifies with recomposition counts.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A scrolling parallax header recomposed the entire detail screen per frame until Modifier.offset(y = dp) became offset { }.

questions.promptHtml: What does Modifier.graphicsLayer do under the hood, and when does it help or hurt? Compare it with alpha, rotate, scale, offset, and clip.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Probes understanding of RenderNode-backed layers, off-recomposition updates, and layer memory/overdraw cost.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: graphicsLayer records the child's drawing into a separate display-list/RenderNode layer so properties like alpha, translation, scale, rotation, clip and shadow can change without re-recording the child's draw commands. The lambda form reads state in the draw/layer-update phase, so animated values skip composition and layout. The cost is that offscreen compositing strategies and layers consume memory and can force offscreen buffers; I avoid blanket use.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Each graphicsLayer modifier allocates (or reuses) a GraphicsLayer that wraps a RenderNode on Android. Property changes (translationX, scaleX, alpha, rotation, shadow, clip) update the render node and the RenderThread re-composites; the child's draw ops are not re-recorded unless its own invalidations occur. This is why transform animation is cheap on graphicsLayer but not on Modifier.padding/size (those change layout).

Notes:

  • alpha < 1 with CompositingStrategy.Auto may need an offscreen buffer when content overlaps (alpha applied to the group, not per draw call). ModulateAlpha skips the offscreen buffer but applies alpha per draw instruction (overlapping children can show through). Offscreen forces a buffer and is required for blend modes in some cases.
  • Modifier.alpha(x), rotate(x), scale(x) take plain values: recomposition per change. The lambda graphicsLayer {} equivalent avoids that.
  • Layout is unaffected: translation does not move the layout bounds nor hit area in the original place (pointer hit-testing uses the transformed position for children inside layers: verify for nested cases), and the parent measures the original size.
  • Setting graphicsLayer with constant values only to "promote a layer" is rarely a win and costs memory.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Pulse(progress: () -> Float) {
    Image(
        painterResource(R.drawable.logo), null,
        Modifier.graphicsLayer {
            val p = progress()          // read in layer phase
            scaleX = 1f + 0.1f * p
            scaleY = 1f + 0.1f * p
            alpha = 1f - 0.3f * p
            compositingStrategy = CompositingStrategy.ModulateAlpha
        }
    )
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Animating width/height with Modifier.size(animatedDp) when a scale would do (layout every frame). Scale changes pixels, not layout; use only when a visual scale is acceptable.
  • Large graphicsLayer on a full-screen container with changing alpha: offscreen buffer the size of the screen each frame.
  • graphicsLayer on every list item to "optimize".
  • Clip with clip = true plus shadow elevation on low-end GPUs: overdraw/cost.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does translation via graphicsLayer change hit-testing? → The child's pointer input follows the transformed position in the usual cases; the parent's measured bounds do not change. Verify edge cases for your own tree.
  2. When use drawWithCache? → When objects (Path, Brush) depend only on size, not animated values.
  3. Why do shadows jank? → shadowElevation plus clip needs an outline; large animated shadows on low-end GPUs cost.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "graphicsLayer for rotation/alpha." Senior: layer = RenderNode, compositing strategy tradeoffs, read phase, and when not to use it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A fade-in on a full-screen map overlay with Modifier.alpha caused offscreen-buffer jank on a low-end device class; changing the strategy fixed it while mid-tier devices never showed it.

questions.promptHtml: How do you draw custom graphics in Compose? Explain Canvas, DrawScope, drawBehind, drawWithContent and drawWithCache, and why drawing code must not allocate.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Basic custom-drawing competence; the allocation point separates people who've profiled draw code.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Canvas(modifier) { } is a composable that gives a DrawScope with size, density and drawing functions (drawCircle, drawRect, drawPath, drawLine, drawImage, drawText via measurer). For decorating an existing composable I use Modifier.drawBehind or drawWithContent. drawWithCache builds size-dependent objects (Path, Brush, shader) once and redraws cheaply. Draw lambdas run on every invalidation, so I never allocate objects in them if I can cache.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
DrawScope is a coordinate space in pixels with origin at top-left; it exposes drawContext.canvas for the raw canvas, and helpers like translate, rotate, scale, clipPath, withTransform, inset. Reads of State inside the lambda register draw-phase observers, so a changed State redraws without recomposition (ties to the phases question).

  • drawBehind { }: draw before content; drawWithContent { drawContent() } lets you draw before/after/instead of the content.
  • drawWithCache { onDrawBehind/onDrawWithContent { } }: the outer block reruns when size changes or read State changes; the inner draw runs every redraw. Use it for Path, Brush.linearGradient(..., size).
  • Text: use rememberTextMeasurer() + drawText, not android.graphics.Canvas calls.
  • Canvas composable size comes from the modifier; with no size it measures to zero (wrap in fillMaxSize or size).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun Ring(progress: () -> Float, modifier: Modifier = Modifier) {
    Canvas(modifier.size(96.dp)) {
        val stroke = Stroke(width = 8.dp.toPx(), cap = StrokeCap.Round)
        drawArc(Color.LightGray, 0f, 360f, useCenter = false, style = stroke)
        drawArc(
            Color(0xFF6650A4), -90f, 360f * progress(),
            useCenter = false, style = stroke
        )
    }
}

fun Modifier.gradientBorder() = drawWithCache {
    val brush = Brush.linearGradient(listOf(Color.Red, Color.Blue), end = Offset(size.width, size.height))
    onDrawBehind { drawRoundRect(brush, cornerRadius = CornerRadius(12.dp.toPx())) }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Creating Path()/Paint()/Brush inside the draw lambda each frame.
  • Mixing dp and px: DrawScope works in px; use dp.toPx().
  • Reading a State with .value in the composable body and passing a Float: recomposes. Pass () -> Float.
  • Forgetting Canvas has no intrinsic size.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. drawBehind vs Canvas? → Same scope; Canvas is a leaf composable with no children, drawBehind decorates any node.
  2. How to draw bitmap with filters? → drawImage(image, colorFilter = ...), or drawIntoCanvas for native.
  3. Accessibility of Canvas? → It has no semantics; add Modifier.semantics { contentDescription = ... } yourself.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use Canvas." Senior: pick the right draw modifier, cache by size, defer reads into the lambda, add semantics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A custom chart allocated 200 Paths per frame during pan; moving them to drawWithCache halved draw time in a System Trace.

questions.promptHtml: How do shared element transitions work in Compose? Explain SharedTransitionLayout, sharedElement vs sharedBounds, the required scopes, and their limitations.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Newer API; tests whether you read the docs and understand overlay rendering, scope plumbing and key design.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: SharedTransitionLayout provides a SharedTransitionScope. Inside it, two composables that exist in different states of an AnimatedContent, AnimatedVisibility or NavHost mark themselves with the same key via rememberSharedContentState(key), and I pass the AnimatedVisibilityScope into Modifier.sharedElement. During the transition the matched content is rendered in an overlay on top of everything and its bounds animate from the source to the target. sharedElement is for the same content (hero image); sharedBounds is for different content sharing a container (container transform), and shows both enter and exit content.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism: the SharedTransitionScope tracks shared content by key. When a key appears in two places and AnimatedVisibilityScope says one is leaving and one entering, the target is "matched" (isMatchFound). The element is drawn in the scope's overlay during the transition so it can escape parent clipping and z-order, and the bounds animate via a BoundsTransform (spring by default; verify). Modifiers before sharedElement supply constraints; modifiers after are laid out with animated constraints, so modifier order must match on both sides. resizeMode = scaleToBounds() or skipToLookaheadSize() makes the child lay out at the target size and scales instead of relayouting.

Docs-listed limitations: no Views interop (including composables wrapping AndroidView, such as Dialog or ModalBottomSheet); ContentScale snaps; no automatic shape-clip animation; for these use sharedBounds + animateEnterExit. Use data-class keys and add item ids in lists. API stability: it shipped as experimental in Compose 1.7 (@ExperimentalSharedTransitionApi); the page I read did not show an experimental marker; verify your Compose version before depending on it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
SharedTransitionLayout {
    AnimatedContent(showDetail, label = "nav") { detail ->
        if (!detail) {
            Row(Modifier.clickable { showDetail = true }) {
                Image(
                    painterResource(R.drawable.cupcake), null,
                    Modifier
                        .sharedElement(
                            rememberSharedContentState(key = "image-$id"),
                            animatedVisibilityScope = this@AnimatedContent
                        )
                        .size(96.dp)
                )
            }
        } else {
            Image(
                painterResource(R.drawable.cupcake), null,
                Modifier
                    .sharedElement(
                        rememberSharedContentState(key = "image-$id"),
                        animatedVisibilityScope = this@AnimatedContent
                    )
                    .fillMaxWidth()
            )
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Same key used by two list rows (all match the wrong row). Include the item id.
  • Different modifier order on source and target: visual jumps.
  • Using it with a Dialog/bottom sheet (AndroidView-backed): not supported.
  • Passing scopes through ten layers instead of CompositionLocal/context parameters (docs discuss the trade-off).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. sharedElement vs sharedBounds? → Same content vs different content in shared area; sharedBounds shows both enter and exit; preferred for Text style changes.
  2. How with Navigation Compose? → NavHost provides the AnimatedVisibilityScope per destination (see docs); place SharedTransitionLayout above the NavHost.
  3. Manual visibility? → sharedElementWithCallerManagedVisibility; remove it from tree after isTransitionActive is false.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use sharedElement with the same key." Senior: overlay mechanism, modifier ordering, key design, interop limits, experimental status.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A gallery transition worked on every row but one: duplicate image URLs were used as keys across two sections.

questions.contextHtml:
A cart screen has a quantity stepper. QA reports: "The number swaps instantly; the slide animation is visible but the old digit changes to the new number while sliding out." The team also sees the price text flicker. Code:

@Composable
fun Stepper(qty: Int, onChange: (Int) -> Unit) {
    Row {
        Button(onClick = { onChange(qty - 1) }) { Text("-") }
        AnimatedContent(
            targetState = qty,
            transitionSpec = {
                slideInVertically { it } togetherWith slideOutVertically { -it }
            },
            label = "qty"
        ) {
            Text("$qty")
        }
        Button(onClick = { onChange(qty + 1) }) { Text("+") }
    }
}

Crash rate is zero, 1.2M DAU, issue reported on 100 percent of devices.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain why it behaves that way, and fix it. What else would you tighten?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Maybe use a different spec" or "add a key". It never notices the lambda ignores its parameter, or explains why exiting content shows the new value.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is qty hoisted and updated synchronously? (rules out async state). Does it happen on rapid taps only? (interruption). Any contentKey set? (changes identity). Min/max clamp behaviours? (not an animation concern but affects the direction logic).
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; it's a visual bug. A one-line fix is safe to hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) lambda ignores its parameter and reads outer qty; (2) rapid taps interrupt and the direction logic is missing; (3) state hoisted incorrectly; (4) size transform clipping.
  4. How I'd verify: Read the code: the content lambda { Text("$qty") } implicitly receives it but reads the closure value. Reproduce in Animation Preview with a fixed label; in Layout Inspector both children exist during the transition and show the same text.
  5. Root cause: AnimatedContent keeps the previous content composed while it exits. That old content's lambda is invoked with the old targetState value, but only if you use the parameter. By reading the outer qty, the exiting child recomposes with the new value, so both children display the new number and the slide looks wrong.
  6. Fix: Use the parameter. Also derive direction from targetState > initialState.
AnimatedContent(
    targetState = qty,
    transitionSpec = {
        val up = targetState > initialState
        (slideInVertically { if (up) it else -it } + fadeIn()) togetherWith
            (slideOutVertically { if (up) -it else it } + fadeOut())
    },
    label = "qty"
) { target ->
    Text("$target")
}
  1. Prevention: A lint-style review rule: in AnimatedContent/Crossfade lambdas, the parameter must be used; the official docs call this out. Add a screenshot test mid-transition using mainClock.autoAdvance = false and advanceTimeBy.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add key(qty) around the Text; that removes the animation structure and recreates the node. I would not set contentKey unless several states map to the same content.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Price flicker too? → Likely a separate AnimatedContent or Crossfade on a string with identical size; check SizeTransform(clip = false) and whether the text is recomposed from a different state.
  • How to avoid sliding on first composition? → AnimatedContent doesn't animate initial composition; check for rememberSaveable reset instead.
  • Tests hang? → Use composeTestRule.mainClock control; infinite animations do not run in tests per the docs.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A promo countdown used the outer variable in an AnimatedContent; no one noticed for months because the default fade looked passable. The animation only "broke" after design switched to a slide.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cannot find the bug; blames spec.
  • Hire: identifies the unused lambda parameter and fixes it, adds direction logic.
  • Strong hire: explains both children composed during transition, tests mid-transition, and discusses contentKey and size transform.

questions.contextHtml:
A shopping home screen has a "flash sale" banner with an animated gradient background and a pulsing badge. After release 8.12, frame time p95 on mid-tier devices (4 GB RAM, 60 Hz) went from 9 ms to 21 ms while the banner is visible; jank rate (JankStats) rose from 2.1 percent to 11 percent. Crash and ANR rates are unchanged. The release also bumped Coil, changed the feed to a LazyColumn, and added the banner. Layout Inspector shows the HomeScreen composable recomposing about 60 times per second, with 40 child composables each recomposing equally. Snippet:

@Composable
fun HomeScreen(vm: HomeViewModel) {
    val state by vm.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    val infinite = rememberInfiniteTransition(label = "sale")
    val hue by infinite.animateFloat(
        0f, 360f,
        infiniteRepeatable(tween(4000, easing = LinearEasing)), label = "hue"
    )
    Column(Modifier.background(Color.hsv(hue, 0.6f, 0.9f))) {
        Banner(state.banner)
        Feed(state.items)
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through diagnosis and the fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames Coil or LazyColumn, suggests @Stable everywhere or removing the animation. Never connects the 60 recompositions per second with the State read location.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does jank only appear while the banner is visible? (isolates banner). Is it all devices or mid-tier only? (GPU/CPU cost). Is it a debug or release build/baseline profile present? (rule out measurement artifacts). Which composables recompose in Layout Inspector: only banner or Feed? (scope).
  2. Immediate mitigation: Feature flag the animated gradient off (static gradient) via remote config; ship in a staged rollout. Keeps the banner, stops the bleeding.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) animated State read in HomeScreen body; its scope contains Feed; (2) Feed(state.items) unstable param so it cannot skip; (3) Coil image requests per recomposition; (4) LazyColumn missing keys. The recomposition count of about 60/s on all 40 children points at (1)+(2).
  4. How I'd verify: Layout Inspector recomposition counts (count rises at frame rate while idle). Compose compiler reports for Feed params (List<Item> unstable if no strong skipping). Perfetto/System Trace: composition slice every frame. Toggle the animation off and compare JankStats in a Macrobenchmark.
  5. Root cause: hue is read in the body of HomeScreen inside Modifier.background(Color.hsv(hue,...)). Every animation frame invalidates the HomeScreen scope and recomposes everything within, including Feed; if Feed's params are unstable (or strong skipping is off, version-dependent: verify) children cannot skip. A background colour change only needs a redraw.
  6. Fix: Short-term: read the animation in the draw phase.
@Composable
fun HomeScreen(vm: HomeViewModel) {
    val state by vm.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    Column {
        SaleBanner(state.banner)
        Feed(state.items)
    }
}

@Composable
private fun SaleBanner(banner: BannerUi) {
    val infinite = rememberInfiniteTransition(label = "sale")
    val hue by infinite.animateFloat(
        0f, 360f,
        infiniteRepeatable(tween(4000, easing = LinearEasing)), label = "hue"
    )
    Box(Modifier.drawBehind { drawRect(Color.hsv(hue, 0.6f, 0.9f)) }) {
        BannerContent(banner)
    }
}

Long-term: confine the animation to the banner (it was applied to the whole Column), make Feed params stable (immutable collection or confirmed strong skipping), and gate by LocalReduceMotion-style setting. 7. Prevention: Macrobenchmark with JankStats for the home scroll; Compose compiler reports checked in CI; code review rule "animated State is read in a lambda modifier". Add recomposition-count assertions in tests for hot screens. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not remove Coil or the LazyColumn on a guess; I would not mark everything @Stable to hide the read issue. A full-screen gradient animation costs GPU fill even when optimal, so I would keep it small and cap with repeatMode/visibility.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Gradient hue interpolates in RGB vs HSV looks off? → Interpolating hue in HSV space is correct for a color wheel; for a two-colour fade use animateColorAsState.
  • Battery complaints? → infiniteRepeatable runs while composed; stop it when offscreen or app backgrounded; pause with a state when the banner scrolls away.
  • Reduced motion setting? → Respect system animation scale (animator duration scale 0): verify how Compose reacts per version; provide an explicit app-level toggle.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A seasonal promo animation shipped hoisted to the screen root "for convenience". Frame time doubled on a device cohort and the fix was a 6-line move of the read plus an extracted composable.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames libraries, proposes rewriting the list.
  • Hire: finds the read location and moves it into a draw lambda; mentions Layout Inspector.
  • Strong hire: also checks stability of Feed, verifies with benchmark, adds prevention, flags accessibility/battery.

questions.contextHtml:
A draggable bottom player sheet uses animateDpAsState for its height. Users report: "dragging feels laggy, like the sheet chases my finger", "on release it sometimes jumps back to its old size", and 7 percent of sessions on low-end devices drop below 30 fps while dragging. Code:

@Composable
fun PlayerSheet() {
    var targetHeight by remember { mutableStateOf(80.dp) }
    val height by animateDpAsState(targetHeight, label = "h")
    Box(
        Modifier
            .height(height)
            .pointerInput(Unit) {
                detectVerticalDragGestures(
                    onDragEnd = { targetHeight = if (targetHeight > 300.dp) 600.dp else 80.dp }
                ) { _, dy -> targetHeight -= dy.toDp() }
            }
    ) { /* player UI */ }
}
questions.promptHtml: Why does it behave this way, and how would you redesign it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the spring stiffness." That treats the symptom; it keeps animation between finger and UI and still relayouts every frame.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the player UI heavy (video surface, lists)? (layout cost). Is the sheet a fixed set of states or free? (anchored drag). Any nested scroll inside? (conflicts).
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise stiffness to StiffnessHigh or use snap() while dragging as a hotfix; ship the proper fix next.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) finger input is routed through a spring-animated state so UI lags behind; (2) onDragEnd reads targetHeight mid-chase and decisions use stale values; (3) Modifier.height relayouts the player content every frame; (4) detectVerticalDragGestures consumes events that the inner scroll needs.
  4. How I'd verify: Perfetto: layout slices every frame; Layout Inspector: recomposition counts per frame; slow motion video; log velocity at onDragEnd (not used).
  5. Root cause: Touch should write the value directly, with animation only after release. Here each dy retargets a spring, so the visible height trails the finger; the fling velocity is thrown away; and the size modifier read in composition body relayouts the full player UI per frame.
  6. Fix: Use Animatable with snapTo while dragging, and animate to the nearest anchor with the release velocity. Move the movement to the layout/graphics phase.
@Composable
fun PlayerSheet() {
    val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()
    val offset = remember { Animatable(0f) } // 0 = expanded, grows downward
    var maxPx by remember { mutableFloatStateOf(0f) }
    val peekPx = with(LocalDensity.current) { 80.dp.toPx() }
    Box(
        Modifier
            .onSizeChanged { maxPx = it.height - peekPx }
            .graphicsLayer { translationY = offset.value }
            .draggable(
                orientation = Orientation.Vertical,
                state = rememberDraggableState { dy ->
                    scope.launch { offset.snapTo((offset.value + dy).coerceIn(0f, maxPx)) }
                },
                onDragStopped = { v ->
                    val projected = offset.value + v * 0.2f // rough projection
                    val target = if (projected > maxPx / 2) maxPx else 0f
                    offset.animateTo(target, spring(), initialVelocity = v)
                }
            )
    ) { /* player UI */ }
}

For multiple anchors with fling and nested scroll, use AnchoredDraggable (foundation) instead of hand-rolling: verify its current API status in your version. 7. Prevention: Gesture UI tests with performTouchInput { swipeUp() } and mainClock; benchmark dragging in Macrobenchmark; code review rule: touch writes via snapTo, release animates. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not animate the player's height per frame; a translation avoids relayout of its subtree. I would not keep animateDpAsState for gestures. Translation via graphicsLayer does not change layout bounds, so insets and nested content must account for it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Need sheet content to resize, not slide? → Use a layout-phase offset/size lambda and accept relayout; keep content simple or use Modifier.layout.
  • Velocity ignored on onDragStopped? → draggable provides velocity; pass it as initialVelocity.
  • Nested lists inside? → Use nestedScroll connection; owned by the input chunk.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "now playing" sheet shipped with a spring-chased drag; the complaint was "feels heavy". Replacing it with direct translation plus a velocity-aware settle fixed it without touching the visuals.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tweaks spring values.
  • Hire: moves to Animatable with snapTo and release animation, mentions velocity.
  • Strong hire: also moves reads out of composition/layout, handles anchors/nested scroll, tests gestures.

questions.contextHtml: A marketplace app (3.5M MAU, Compose 1.8 per the BOM; verify your own) wants a hero transition from a grid of product cards to a detail screen. Prototype: SharedTransitionLayout wrapping a NavHost; image uses sharedElement(rememberSharedContentState("image")). Findings: all product cards animate to whichever detail opens; the title text blinks between two font weights; on 2 GB RAM devices the transition drops to about 25 fps; the "Add to cart" bottom sheet over the detail screen sometimes flashes. Product managers want it on every launch next sprint.
questions.promptHtml: How do you design and ship this safely?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Just add the modifier everywhere." It misses unique keys, sharedBounds for text, overlay behaviour, interop limits, device cost and a rollout plan.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is detail loaded async (placeholder size mismatch)? Same image resolution in both places? (decoding cost). Does the sheet use ModalBottomSheet? (AndroidView-based per docs). Which minimum device must hit 60 fps? (budget).
  2. Immediate mitigation: Keep the prototype behind a flag; default off for low-end devices so the nav still uses a plain fade.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) the key is a constant string so every card matches; (2) text uses sharedElement while the style changes (weight), which docs say should be sharedBounds; (3) full-size image decode during transition on weak devices; (4) bottom sheet is a window/AndroidView-backed component which is not supported with shared transitions per docs.
  4. How I'd verify: Run on a resizable emulator and a real 2 GB device; System Trace for the transition frames; Layout Inspector for recompositions of the grid during transition; check logs for decoded bitmap sizes.
  5. Root cause: Keys: "image" is not unique, so the transition matches by key and the last-registered item wins. Text weight change needs sharedBounds. Frame drops: the overlay draws full-resolution content while the grid beneath still composes. Sheet flash: the unsupported interop case.
  6. Fix: Key by data class, with productId and element type; use sharedBounds for the title and card container; apply the same modifier order on both sides; request the same image size (memory cache key) in both places so the second decode is skipped; keep a plain ModalBottomSheet out of the shared scope or replace with an in-hierarchy sheet.
data class ProductKey(val id: Long, val type: ProductElement)
enum class ProductElement { Image, Title, Container }

with(sharedTransitionScope) {
    Image(
        painter, null,
        Modifier.sharedElement(
            rememberSharedContentState(ProductKey(p.id, ProductElement.Image)),
            animatedVisibilityScope = animatedVisibilityScope
        )
    )
}
  1. Prevention: A test that opens detail for item 5 and asserts only that image matches (isMatchFound can be logged); benchmark the transition with Macrobenchmark on a low-tier device; a remote kill switch.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not ship it to every device on day one; low-end gets a fade. I would not animate shapes or ContentScale expecting automatic behaviour (docs list these as unsupported). I'd verify the API's experimental status for our Compose version and pin versions accordingly.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Back gesture (predictive back) interplay? → Verify your Navigation Compose version's support for seekable transitions with shared elements; test manually.
  • Pager of images in detail? → Only the visible page should carry the shared key.
  • Process death on detail? → Shared transition is only a visual layer; state restoration is the nav chunk's concern.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A hero transition looked flawless in a demo with 5 items and shipped; with real data duplicates in the carousel (same SKU twice) matched the wrong card. Item position was added to the key.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: puts the same modifier on both screens and stops.
  • Hire: unique keys, sharedBounds for text, modifier order.
  • Strong hire: interop limits, low-end strategy, rollout flag, benchmark, API stability awareness.

questions.contextHtml: A feed shows skeleton shimmer placeholders: 12 visible skeleton cards, each with its own rememberInfiniteTransition driving a gradient Brush created in the composable body and applied with Modifier.background(brush). Battery dashboards show a 3 percent regression in foreground drain on the loading screen; JankStats reports 14 percent janky frames during the first 2 s of loading on low-end devices; UI tests that await idle now time out intermittently (about 8 percent of runs). Network is slow so skeletons stay visible 4 to 8 seconds.
questions.promptHtml: What's wrong and how do you fix it, including the tests?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make the animation shorter" or "remove shimmer". Doesn't identify N independent infinite transitions, composition-phase brush creation, or test idling.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the shimmer shared visually across cards (sweeping across the screen) or per card? Does it stop when the screen is backgrounded? Which test framework idling is timing out (Compose test waitForIdle vs Espresso)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reduce visible skeletons to what fits the viewport and add a remote flag to switch to a static placeholder on low-end devices.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) 12 infinite transitions each invalidating a composition scope per frame, creating a new Brush each time; (2) shimmer brush covers large areas at full resolution (GPU fill); (3) animation continues when offscreen/backgrounded; (4) test idling confused by infinite animation (the docs say infiniteRepeatable does not run under the ComposeTestRule, but Espresso/idling or other waits may not follow that rule: verify).
  4. How I'd verify: Layout Inspector counts on skeleton composables; trace: per-frame composition slices; energy profiler or battery historian on the loading screen; Macrobenchmark startup-to-content with JankStats.
  5. Root cause: Per-item animation state is read in composition, so each frame recomposes 12 scopes and allocates 12 brushes; there is no shared clock.
  6. Fix: One transition at the container, one float read in the draw phase, and shared by all skeletons; build the brush with the offset applied in the draw lambda.
@Composable
fun ShimmerHost(content: @Composable (shimmer: () -> Float) -> Unit) {
    val t = rememberInfiniteTransition(label = "shimmer")
    val x by t.animateFloat(
        0f, 1f,
        infiniteRepeatable(tween(1200, easing = LinearEasing)), label = "x"
    )
    content { x }
}

fun Modifier.shimmer(progress: () -> Float) = drawWithCache {
    val base = Color(0xFFE0E0E0); val hi = Color(0xFFF5F5F5)
    onDrawBehind {
        val w = size.width
        val start = -w + 3 * w * progress()
        drawRect(
            Brush.linearGradient(
                listOf(base, hi, base),
                start = Offset(start, 0f), end = Offset(start + w, 0f)
            )
        )
    }
}

Stop the transition when the host leaves composition or the lifecycle is below STARTED; skip it entirely when the system animator scale is 0 (verify how to read it for your min SDK). 7. Prevention: A reusable shimmer in the design system; a benchmark for loading states; lint-like review check: "no rememberInfiniteTransition inside list items". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: One shared clock means all skeletons pulse in sync (design usually likes it). I would not use Lottie for a plain shimmer; I'd not disable shimmer globally for a regression limited to low-end devices.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Shimmer on a LazyColumn of skeletons? → Same shared progress; draw-phase read means scrolling items don't recompose.
  • How to test visually? → Screenshot tests with the progress parameter pinned ({ 0.3f }), which is why the modifier takes a lambda.
  • Reduce GPU fill? → Limit area, avoid full-screen gradients, use solid-colour fallback on low-end.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A loading screen was the most-seen screen in the app on slow networks, so a shimmer cost there outweighed the home screen's total energy budget. Fixing it improved a battery metric more than a month of backend work.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: shortens animation or removes it.
  • Hire: shares one transition, reads in draw phase, avoids per-frame brush allocation.
  • Strong hire: lifecycle/offscreen stopping, test strategy, device-tier flagging, measurement with benchmark and battery tools.
